newsitem.title: UK: Copper prices push higher as stocks erode further.
newsitem.headline: Copper prices push higher as stocks erode further.

text.p: Copper prices surged on Tuesday as inventories fell to fresh six-year lows amid fears that output could be hurt in the world's biggest producer Chile.
Prices for delivery in three months touched the highest level in 2-1/2 months at $2,057 after stocks in London Metal Exchange (LME) warehouses continued a series of falls.
LME stocks eroded by 4,225 tonnes to 109,175 tonnes, the lowest level since August 1990.
The premium for prompt metal soared as traders scrambled for material, rising to nearly $100.
Many analysts, however, were perplexed since the price rise is still much below the year's peak around $2,715 in May.
Prices ended $33 stronger at $2,045 per tonne.
"It is very hard to make sense of this. It looks like somebody is trying to keep it in a range," a senior trader said.
Some analysts believe stocks are not being consumed but moved out of LME warehouses into hidden stockpiles.
"Traders continue to smell a rat and remain very wary about putting too much trust into the LME stock erosion," an analyst said.
The market was watching closely developments in central Chile where the worst drought in 30 years threatened the water-dependent copper processing industry.
So far output has not been affected but officials said the coming summer months in the southern hemisphere would be critical.
Aluminium was only slightly stronger, closing $6.50 firmer at $1,454.50 per tonne.
In other markets, gold chugged higher, recovering further above the psychological $380 per ounce mark, inspired by investment funds closing out bearish positions.
Prices ended off their highs, but still finished with a gain of $1.00.
In Chicago, wheat opened higher as the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) trimmed its stock level forecasts for the 1996-1997 season.
Prices have slid from record highs over $7.00 per bushel earlier in the year as hefty harvests have come in.
Shortly after the opening, wheat on the Chicago Board of Exchange for December delivery was seven cents firmer at 390-1/2 cents per bushel.
But corn and soybeans eased as the USDA raised output estimates.
Business was slack in coffee as market participants made their way to Costa Rica for a trade meeting while cocoa slipped through a technical support level, continuing its recent downtrend.
Cocoa closed in London 12 stg weaker at 925 stg after hitting a new seven month low of 923 stg.
